seasoned: For a steady supply, stagger sowings: presoak and start a fresh tray every 4 to 7 days rather than one big tray at once. Indoors there is no season, so the cadence is limited only by your tray count and counter space.

beginner: Sunflower sprouts, usually called sunflower shoots, are baby sunflower plants you grow indoors from black oil sunflower seed and cut young, about 8 to 14 days after planting. The steps are always the same: soak the seed for 8 to 12 hours, scatter it thickly on a shallow tray of coconut coir or seed-starting mix, cover the tray with a weight to keep it dark for a few days while it sprouts, then uncover it into bright light to green up, then snip and eat. Sunflower has two quirks compared with leafy microgreens: the big seed needs a soak, and the black shells stick to the leaves, so you press the tray with a weight to help them fall off and rub or rinse off any that remain. In return you get a nutty, crunchy, filling shoot that is a favorite for its texture. There is no outdoor season or weather to worry about, so they grow the same way no matter where you live.
seasoned: Sunflower sprouts, better called sunflower shoots, are the young seedlings of Helianthus annuus grown indoors from black oil sunflower seed and cut at the plump-cotyledon stage, roughly 8 to 14 days after sowing. The cycle is a short, repeatable indoor one: presoak the seed 8 to 12 hours, sow it densely on a shallow tray of coir or seed-starting mix, germinate under a covered, weighted tray in the dark for about 3 to 4 days, then uncover into light to green up and cut. Two things set sunflower apart from leafier microgreens: the large seed must be soaked, and the black hulls cling to the cotyledons, so growers weight the tray to help them shed and rub or rinse the stragglers off before harvest. The payoff is a nutty, crunchy, substantial shoot that many growers keep for texture alone. Because there is no frost, season, or hardiness zone involved, the same tray grows identically on a windowsill anywhere.

beginner: Your sunflower shoots are ready when the seed leaves are full and open and before the first true leaves start to show, usually about 9 to 12 days after planting. Brush or rinse off any leftover black shells, then snip the shoots at the base with clean scissors and eat them fresh. They do not grow back, so start a new tray each time.
seasoned: Cut at the plump-cotyledon stage, typically about 9 to 12 days from sowing (the workable window runs 8 to 14), before the first true leaves expand and the stems fiber up. Snip at the base with clean scissors; the stand will not regrow, so the tray is a single cut. Rub or rinse off any clinging black hulls first.
